name: 台湾国语 (Taiwan Mandarin)
summary: Taiwan Mandarin (國語) is written in Traditional characters and differs from Mainland Putonghua in vocabulary, sentence-final particles and some sounds. Round 2 re-read English Wikipedia's Taiwanese Mandarin page in full detail and opened 15 Wiktionary entries for Taiwan-labelled words and particles, plus one phonetics paper (Chuang et al. 2019). The Ministry of Education dictionaries and a Chinese-Wikipedia comparison list were unreachable, so MOE dictionary entries were not confirmed. 土豆/馬鈴薯 is a false friend and kept corrected. Hokkien loans (歹勢, 夭壽, 古錐, 黑白講, 阿-) are marked as loans, not neutral Mandarin.

grammar.standard: 了啊 (completed or changed, plus emotion)
grammar.condition: English Wikipedia: in Taiwan 啦 is very common and can follow 了; it carries irritation or complaint (睡覺了啦！明天還要上課耶！). The source also traces the use to Hokkien 'la'. Wiktionary says in Mandarin it is a contraction of 了 + 啊.
Friendly repeated urging: 再吃一碗啦！ (English Wikipedia).
啦 added to push back on a claim. English Wikipedia example 不可能啦。
Prefix 阿 adds familiarity to a kinship term or name, from Hokkien (阿妹, 阿英).

Wiktionary: in Taiwan Mandarin and Taiwanese Hokkien a final particle that seeks agreement or confirmation ('right?'). Hokkien reading honnh. No example sentence given on the page; the example below is constructed.
grammar.romanization: zhè ge hěn hǎo xiào hōu?

grammar.condition: English Wikipedia lists hoⁿh [hɔ̃ʔ] as a Hokkien loan particle asking for agreement ('..., all right?'), and says it may also express a command. Written forms vary (乎, 厚, 齁).

grammar.dialect: 欸 at the start of a sentence
grammar.condition: Wiktionary lists 欸 as an interjection with tone-coded uses: 1st tone to get attention (欸，我告訴你一個秘密), 2nd tone surprise (欸，他怎麼走了), 3rd tone objection, 4th tone agreement. Taiwanese Hokkien reading --eh.
grammar.romanization: ēi, wǒ gàosù nǐ yí ge mìmì

grammar.condition: Wiktionary: 喔 as a Mandarin particle conveys realization or surprise (ō); in Taiwanese Hokkien it is an emphatic final particle used for requests, listed as the Hokkien counterpart of 吧 for Taipei and Kaohsiung. Taiwan Mandarin itself is shown with 吧 in that table, so treat 喔 in Mandarin lines as Hokkien-influenced colour. No sentence example on the page.

English Wikipedia's 啦 example uses 耶 at the end of 明天還要上課耶 as a reminder ('you know, there's class tomorrow'). Wiktionary describes a separate 耶 particle (yē) of joy or surprise, chiefly in Internet slang, e.g. 好耶. The functions overlap, so use 耶 only for reminders and cheerful reactions.
English Wikipedia: 而已 is common in Taiwanese colloquial speech, while Beijing-style 呗, 嚜, 罷了 are rare there.

Taxi. Wiktionary: chiefly Taiwan; 小黃 is the colloquial 'yellow car'. Hong Kong 的士, Mainland 出租車.

Taiwan: scooter or motorcycle (short for 機器腳踏車). Mainland 摩托车 mótuōchē. WARNING: 機車 as an adjective is Taiwan slang 'a pain in the neck, picky, annoying' (你很機車), derived from a Hokkien rude word. Mainland 机车 = locomotive.
Pineapple. Wiktionary: mainly Taiwan; Hong Kong and Guangzhou say 菠蘿.

English Wikipedia: slang from military-dependents' villages (眷村). Slang, not neutral.
English Wikipedia: slang for a woman or girlfriend from the same 眷村 vocabulary. Can sound crude. Avoid unless the character is a rough speaker.
From Hokkien 烏白講; talk nonsense.
English Wikipedia gives the Hokkien sense 'worship or ritual'. Its casual goodbye use is not confirmed in the sources I opened.
English Wikipedia: the letter Q marks a springy, chewy texture, from Hokkien khiū. Used for food.

Wiktionary: Hokkien interjection 'excuse me, sorry', adjective 'embarrassed'. The page lists 拍謝 as a Mandarin-based respelling. It is a Hokkien loan, so it fits casual, local or older speakers more than formal speech. Taiwan Mandarin equivalents shown on that page: 不好意思, 對不起.
Wiktionary: in Taiwan an adjective 'wicked, miserable'; Hokkien slang interjection 'damn'. Originally means to die young, so it can read as a curse. Casual exclamations only.
Wiktionary lists 古錐 'cute, adorable' as a Hokkien adjective (Xiamen, Quanzhou, Zhangzhou, Tainan, Singapore). Its use inside Taiwan Mandarin was not confirmed. Prefer 可愛 in Mandarin lines.

vocabulary.dialect: 里長 / 郵差 / 次長
vocabulary.note: English Wikipedia: terms from pre-1949 China still used in Taiwan; 先生, 小姐, 太太, 老闆 also used as titles more freely.

particles.function: Very common in Taiwan. Uses listed by English Wikipedia: irritation or complaint, friendly urging, rebuttal. Wiktionary: a contraction of 了 + 啊 in Mandarin; the Hokkien la shows reluctance, 'all right already'. Needs different pitch in each use.
particles.example: 睡覺了啦！ / 再吃一碗啦！ / 不可能啦。

particles.function: Reminder or joyful reaction at the end of a clause. English Wikipedia's complaint example ends with it; Wiktionary calls the joy/surprise use chiefly Internet slang.
Seeks agreement or confirmation ('right?'), Taiwan Mandarin and Taiwanese Hokkien.
Hokkien loan: asks for agreement ('..., all right?'); may express a command.

Mandarin sense: realization or surprise. Hokkien sense: emphatic final particle in requests. Taiwan Mandarin tables show 吧 where Hokkien uses 喔, so in Mandarin lines this is a Hokkien-flavoured softener.
Interjection at the start of a sentence: attention (1st tone), surprise (2nd), objection (3rd), agreement (4th).
Colloquially common in Taiwan, where Beijing-style 呗, 嚜, 罷了 are rare.
Common in Beijing Mandarin and rare in Taiwan Mandarin. Do not use them as Taiwan markers.

pronunciation.rule: Retroflex initials zh, ch, sh are often read as z, c, s (dental), in most situations. A 2019 study of 331 speakers from 120 places found merging is less common in big cities than in the surrounding areas; the study ties the merging to contact with Hokkien.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Do not say all zh/ch/sh flat in every line. For a Taipei or highly educated character keep retroflex; for a rural or Hokkien-speaking character flatten a part of them.
pronunciation.example: 知道 zhīdào → zīdào (illustrative); 是 shì → sì (illustrative)

pronunciation.rule: Final -ing/-eng often become -in/-en, and -n and -ng can merge, so 爭 zhēng and 真 zhēn may sound the same.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Make 'ing' lighter, like 'in'. 'eng' ≈ 'en'. Use this on casual lines only.
pronunciation.example: 爭 = 真; 英 yīng ≈ yīn

pronunciation.rule: The r- initial may be realized as [ɹ] (English Wikipedia). The page does not say r becomes l or z.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Use a soft, light r that is not strongly curled. Do not convert r to l.

pronunciation.rule: Neutral tone is less frequent: final syllables often keep their full tone (但是 dànshì, 先生 xiānshēng). Nouns ending in 子 or 頭 still soften (孩子 is not háizǐ).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Give the last syllable of 但是, 先生, 知道 a clear tone. Keep 子 light.

pronunciation.rule: Erhua is very rare, common in Beijing. Taiwan retroflex sounds and tones are described as less prominent and flatter (zh.wikipedia: 國語捲舌音較普通話不明顯，兒化音較少，聲調也較平緩).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Drop the r-ending (玩儿 → 玩). Keep pitch movement smaller than Beijing speech.

pronunciation.rule: The vowel ㄛ is read as a half-open [ɔ] (Mainland closer [o]); after ㄅㄆㄇㄈ the ㄥ is read near [oŋ].
pronunciation.actor_tip: Say 'o' in 我, 多, 波 a bit more open and 'eng' after b/p/m/f (like 風, 夢) as 'ong'.

pronunciation.rule: About 13% of character readings differ between Taiwan and Mainland standards (a figure cited to Li 2002 on zh.wikipedia).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Check readings in the Ministry of Education dictionary when a line has unusual characters.

tones_intonation.rule: 啦 changes meaning by pitch: irritation uses a lower, extended pitch; urging a bright, lightly rising pitch; rebuttal a short, flat denial. The three functions are listed by English Wikipedia; the pitch descriptions are my acting suggestions, not verified phonetics.
欸 has four tone-coded uses: tone 1 attention, tone 2 surprise, tone 3 objection, tone 4 agreement (Wiktionary).
Taiwan Mandarin pitch movement is described as flatter than Beijing speech (zh.wikipedia), and the neutral tone appears less often, so the rhythm is steadier and each syllable is a bit more separate.
Final 齁 and 喔 invite a response and normally take a slightly raised or held pitch. This is my acting suggestion; no phonetic source was opened.

sub_regions.region: 台北 / 大都市 (Taipei and other metropolitan cities)
sub_regions.features: A study of 331 speakers from 120 places found that merging of dental and retroflex sibilants (zh/ch/sh → z/c/s) is less common in metropolitan cities than in the surrounding areas. For acting: a Taipei character keeps more retroflex sounds.

sub_regions.region: 南部 / 中部 (Southern and Central Taiwan)
sub_regions.features: The same study implies more merging outside big cities. A separate common claim that Hokkien influence is stronger in the south and centre comes from a search summary of an archived Wikipedia page that I did not open, so it is unverified. Hokkien loan words (歹勢, 夭壽, 黑白講, 阿-prefix) should be tied to the character's background, not to a region.
Everything in this file describes Taiwan Mandarin broadly. A heavy Hokkien-accented Mandarin (台灣國語) is a stereotype that can read as a caricature; avoid it unless the script demands it.

common_mistakes: Putting 啦 at the end of every sentence. It marks irritation, urging or rebuttal, and each needs a different pitch.
Converting 馬鈴薯 into 土豆. In Taiwan 土豆 is peanut.
Using 機車 for 'motorcycle' without noticing the adjective meaning 'annoying' in a line of dialogue, and the reverse.
Using Hokkien loans (歹勢, 夭壽, 古錐, 黑白講, 阿妹) in formal or narrated lines, or for every character.
Using Mainland words (网络, 软件, 打印, 视频, 信息, 出租车) in Taiwan lines.
Using 呗, 嚜, 罷了 or erhua as Taiwan markers. They are rare there.
Flattening zh/ch/sh in every word until the speech sounds like a parody of 台灣國語.
Writing 古錐 or 拍謝 as everyday Mandarin. Wiktionary shows them as Hokkien.
generational_notes: Hokkien loans such as 歹勢 and 夭壽 are generally more at home with older or more local speakers. This is general knowledge and no opened source gives age data.
耶 as a joyful reaction is called chiefly Internet slang by Wiktionary, so younger-sounding.
A search result summary (NCCU thesis, not opened) said young speakers vary in the realization of tone 2, more among Hokkien-Mandarin bilinguals. Unverified.
conversion_guidelines: Write in Traditional characters, as natural spoken Taiwan Mandarin like film dialogue. Keep full tones on 但是, 先生, 知道.
Swap Mainland vocabulary for the Taiwan form: 网络→網路, 软件→軟體, 打印→列印, 视频→影片, 信息→資訊, 地铁→捷運, 出租车→計程車, 摩托车→機車, 盒饭→便當, 菠萝→鳳梨, 便利店→超商, 土豆(potato)→馬鈴薯, 公交车→公車.
Add 啦 to at most one or two lines per speech, matched to emotion (complaint, urging, rebuttal). Use 齁 or 耶 once at most, 欸 for an attention-getting start.
Use Hokkien loans (歹勢, 夭壽, 黑白講, 阿-) sparingly and only for casual or local characters.
Do not add erhua, 呗, 嚜 or 罷了.
Soften zh/ch/sh only through actor notes, not in the written line. Note that merging is less common in big cities.
Flag every constructed line and unconfirmed item (古錐, 泡麵, 拜拜 as goodbye, 乎) for a Taiwan native or the MOE dictionary.

open_questions: Ministry of Education 《國語辭典》 and 《臺灣閩南語常用詞辭典》 entries could not be opened (404 or JavaScript pages). Check 歹勢, 夭壽, 古錐 and the particles there.
Whether 喔, 齁, 耶, 欸 are used as often in Taiwan Mandarin speech as in Hokkien; Wiktionary labels several of them as Hokkien.
The pitch descriptions for 啦, 齁, 喔 in tones_intonation are acting suggestions, not phonetics.
古錐 as a word used within Taiwan Mandarin was not confirmed: Wiktionary treats it as Hokkien.
泡麵, 拜拜 as 'goodbye', 搭 vs 坐 for taking the MRT and 小黃 usage were not confirmed in an opened source.
Whether the north-south pronunciation difference is also affected by sex, age and social class: the study mentions limited prior work.
Check a Taiwanese native on constructed lines: 歹勢啦, 夭壽喔, 這支影片很好笑齁.
